paragraphs.heading: What predation is
paragraphs.text: Predation is an interaction between living things in which one, the predator, kills and eats another, the prey. It belongs to a family of feeding habits that also includes parasitism and micropredation, which usually leave the host alive, and parasitoidism, which always kills it in the end. Predation is different from scavenging, which means eating only what is already dead, though many predators such as jackals and hyenas scavenge when they get the chance. It also overlaps with plant eating, since seed predators and animals that destroy fruit count as predators.

paragraphs.heading: Where the line falls
paragraphs.text: The boundaries are not always clear. A parasitoid, for example an ichneumon wasp, places its eggs in or on a host, and the larvae that hatch eat the host until it dies; zoologists usually call this a kind of parasitism. One way to tell them apart is that a predator catches many prey over its life, while a parasitoid larva has just one. Animals that graze on phytoplankton count as predators because they kill what they eat, while herbivores that browse leaves do not, since their plants usually survive. Eating seeds or eggs counts too, because each one is a whole living organism.

paragraphs.heading: Hunting strategies
paragraphs.text: To eat, a predator must search for, chase and kill its prey, a sequence called the foraging cycle. It has to decide where to look, and once it finds prey, whether to go after it or wait for something better. Pursuit predators actively seek out and chase prey, while ambush predators wait for a chance, often using stealth or aggressive mimicry to get close enough to strike. Some animals hunt only now and then: several mainly plant-eating rodents add invertebrates to their diet when the chance comes.

paragraphs.heading: The hunter's toolkit
paragraphs.text: Most obligate carnivores are built for hunting. They may have keen sight, hearing or smell for finding prey, and sharp claws or jaws to grip, kill and cut it up. Big cats and other large carnivores usually need physical strength to bring down large prey. Stealth, endurance, intelligence and social behaviour can also make hunting more efficient.

paragraphs.heading: Prey fight back
paragraphs.text: Predation pushes hard on how prey evolve. Prey develop defences such as warning colours, alarm calls, camouflage, copying well-defended species, and protective spines and chemicals. Predator and prey can be caught in an evolutionary arms race, where adaptations on one side are met by counter-adaptations on the other. Predation has been a major force in evolution since at least the Cambrian period.

paragraphs.heading: Predators everywhere
paragraphs.text: Predators are not only mammals and birds. Among insects, mantids, dragonflies and lacewings hunt, and so do spiders, scorpions and centipedes. In the sea, most cnidarians such as jellyfish, along with comb jellies, sea stars and flatworms, are predators, and crustaceans are eaten by nearly all cephalopods, such as octopuses, squid and cuttlefish. Even some plants, such as the Venus fly trap and the sundew, eat insects, some fungi trap nematodes with tightening rings or sticky structures, and many protozoa and bacteria prey on other microorganisms.
